en: The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-varṣā-vastu*,
one fascicle,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing under Imperial Decree during the Great Tang Dynasty.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, observed the three-month rains retreat at this residence.
At that time, there were many bhikṣus who, during the summer retreat, traveled through various human settlements elsewhere; they failed to guard themselves properly and killed insects and ants.
At that time, all the non-Buddhists gave rise to derision and spoke thus:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no compassion; they travel about during the summer retreat, killing various insects and creatures, no different from worldly folk."
Yet even birds and beasts, during the four months [of the rainy season], still remain in their nests and burrows and do not venture far outside.
How is it that these shaven-headed śramaṇas do not observe the *varṣā* retreat, do not know how to withdraw themselves, and do not settle in one place?
"Since there is no established rule, who then will provide food and clothing as alms here?
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "On account of this matter, I now establish the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) for bhikṣus: they shall dwell in one place for the three months."
When the bhikṣus had heard these words, they did not know how to perform the method for the rains retreat (varṣā).
The Buddha said:

"First, on the fifteenth day of the fifth month, you should sprinkle and sweep the dwelling place until it is pure, and smear the ground with cow dung. Then, gather all the bedding and requisites in one place, including even the basins for washing the feet."
Once the assembly has gathered, one bhikṣu should be appointed as the custodian of bedding and furniture.
If he possesses five qualities, he should not be appointed. What are these five?
That is to say, one who possesses craving, ill will, fear, or delusion, and does not know whether bedding and seating have been distributed or not.
One who is the opposite of these five qualities is the one who should be appointed.
He should be appointed in this manner:
Having spread the mats for sitting and struck the *gandī* gong, he announced to the assembled community, first asking a certain bhikṣu:
"Are you able to distribute the bedding for the Saṃgha during the summer retreat?"
He replies, “I can. Then,
one bhikṣu should first perform the formal announcement (jñapti), followed by the ritual act (karman).
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu, so-and-so, wishes to distribute bedding for the Saṃgha during the summer rains retreat.

If the Saṃgha deems the time right and grants its consent, the Saṃgha should authorize that the Saṃgha now appoints this bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the bhikṣu to distribute bedding for the Saṃgha during the summer rains retreat.”
The motion is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, [Name], wishes to distribute bedding and seating for the Saṃgha observing the summer retreat."
The Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu so-and-so to distribute bedding for the Saṃgha during the summer retreat.

If the venerable ones consent to the appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so to distribute bedding for the Saṃgha during the summer retreat, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.

"The Saṃgha has already authorized [the name] as the bhikṣu to distribute bedding for the Saṃgha during the summer retreat; the Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence. Thus do I now uphold this."
The Buddha said: "I shall now establish for the bhikṣus the method for distributing bedding.

The person appointed as the administrator should first prepare the voting tallies for the Saṃgha; next, on the following day, he should arrange the seats, strike the ghaṇṭā, and perform the formal announcement."

Each tally should have flowers tied to both ends and be polished and adorned with fragrant clay; they are placed within a bamboo box, thoroughly perfumed with incense, and covered with white cotton cloth. Each tally is one cubit in length and is set before the seat of the presiding elder.
Next, he proclaimed the formal injunction: "Listen, venerable Saṃgha!
Regarding all the established rules for this residence, if you, venerable sirs, are willing to observe this rainy-season retreat without transgression, you should take up a tally."

O assembly of bhikṣus, during this summer retreat, you should not further reproach one another by saying that someone has violated their views, violated their precepts, violated their right conduct, or violated their right livelihood.

If those who possess benevolence and the like perceive that an offense has been committed, they may discuss the matter at this very time; it is not appropriate to bring such matters to light during the summer retreat, for it would disturb the bhikṣus and prevent them from dwelling in peace and happiness.
Having spoken thus, he next proceeded to distribute the bedding and utensils.

He ordered one bhikṣu to hold a tray of counting-sticks (śalākā) before him, while another who was to collect the sticks followed behind with an empty tray. The Great Master and Teacher first placed one stick down, then stood before the Elder (sthavira). The Elder, in turn, should move slightly from his seat, squat down, join his palms, and receive the stick.
Then, remaining composed, he places it upon an empty plate.
In this manner, the process continues in succession until the end of the row.
If there is a *śrāmaṇera* whose person does not come, the *ācārya* or *upādhyāya* shall take his voting tally (*śalākā*) on his behalf.
Next, take the tally-sticks of the deity who protects the monastery.
Once they have all been distributed, one should count them and announce to the assembly:
"In this residence, there are this many bhikṣus currently receiving voting tallies and this many śrāmaṇeras.
Then, the bhikṣu distributing bedding and utensils takes all the keys and places them before the senior monk (sthavira), saying:
"Venerable Sir!"
"In such-and-such a room there are robes and provisions; if you so desire, take them.
If the senior monk does not take that room, it should be offered to the second senior monk.
If the second senior monk takes this room, the former residence should be given to the third senior monk.
In this manner, it should be passed on in succession until the end of the Saṃgha assembly.
When the first senior elder sees that he is giving [an item] to the second senior elder, if he then requests it again, it should not be given at the time of the first request;
it need not be given at the time of the second request either;
however, it should be given at the time of the third request, though the senior elder incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

In this manner, it is passed on successively until it reaches the last member of the assembly; as previously stated, they incur an offense against the Dharma (vayadharmika-āpatti) in due order, which should be understood according to the above.
However, all the dwellings and rooms within the residence were entirely distributed.
When visiting bhikṣus arrived and there were no rooms available to give them,
the World-Honored One said:
"One room along with its bedding should be set aside for visiting bhikṣus."
At that time, the bhikṣus consequently left [their lodgings] beneath the gate-houses, in front of the corridors and eaves, and on the walkways for the visiting bhikṣus. The Buddha said:
"One should not leave [one's lodgings] beneath the gate-houses, nor even on the walkways, for visiting bhikṣus."
"This location is an abode for various birds; it is not a dwelling place for humans.
The Buddha said, "One bhikṣu should be appointed to oversee the Saṃgha’s offerings, and a separate room should be set aside to provide bedding and furnishings."
However, that bhikṣu should personally guard all his belongings and further inspect for insects and bee nests.
If bees have emerged from the nest, they should be removed immediately;
if the larvae have not yet emerged, he should suspend them with a thread and place them elsewhere, so that once they have grown, they will depart of their own accord.
If visiting bhikṣus arrive, bedding and requisites should be provided.
If there are few people, each person shall be given one set.
If there are many people, two shall share one, or three may share one.
There were some senior *bhikṣus* who, having obtained heavy woolen rugs, found them difficult to move and did not know what to do.
The Buddha said:
"If a senior *bhikṣu* is unable to move [the rug], there should be a junior *bhikṣu* made to rely upon him."
Once the bedding has been distributed, one should immediately inform them:

"If you have no personal mattress, you must not lie down recklessly; nor should you use small items—such as those that are soiled, greasy, torn, or thin—to substitute for the communal monastic bedding."
The person in charge of affairs shall inspect the rooms in turn; seeing those who act improperly, they shall punish them according to the circumstances.
If the offender is of young age, they should inform the two teachers and have them reprimand him.
The bhikṣu appointed to inspect the lodgings shall, on the fifteenth day of every month, tour the rooms and observe them.
If anyone is found using bedding or furniture in an improper manner, he shall inform the Saṃgha and confiscate the items, while also subjecting the offender to disciplinary measures.
If one relies upon a preceptor’s disciple, one should inform that preceptor and have them collect the bedding and requisites.
When the community has assembled, one should announce:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"In this present residence, there being so many people, you should rely upon [Name] as the donor and [Name] village as the place for alms-seeking.
With [Name] as the administrator of affairs and [Name] as the attendant for the sick, you should observe the rains retreat in this residence."
At that time, the bhikṣus should inspect the neighboring villages and alms-rounding areas.
Having completed their observations, those who feel affection for a particular place should each think to themselves:
"I am fit to observe the rains retreat in this location."
He does not give rise to distress regarding his fellow practitioners of the holy life;
even if such distress should arise, he is able to quickly eliminate it.
He causes all happiness that has not yet arisen to arise, and encourages that which has already arisen to further increase.
In the village alms-rounds, no weariness or hardship arises.
If I fall ill, there will be attendants to serve me, providing me with medicine and whatever food and drink are required, all of which shall be fully supplied.

Having formed this thought, one should enter a secluded place, stand before a single bhikṣu, fully observe the proper deportment, pay respects according to seniority, squat down with palms joined, and speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me!"
Today, on the sixteenth day of the fifth month, the Saṃgha enters the summer retreat.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], likewise enter the summer retreat on the sixteenth day of the fifth month.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall observe the three-month summer retreat within the boundary of this residence.
With [Name] as my patron, [Name] as my attendant for affairs, and [Name] as my caregiver, I shall remain at this residence and repair whatever is dilapidated, cracked, or broken.
"I shall observe the rains retreat here this summer.
The second and third times he should speak likewise.
The bhikṣu being addressed should say:
"Avoca. He replied, "Sādhu."

"If there are causes and conditions such that one cannot participate in the preceding *anvārambhaṇa* (early) retreat, it is permitted to undertake the subsequent *anvārambhaṇa* (late) retreat; this should be performed according to the previous procedure.
Once the retreat has been entered, one must not stay overnight outside the boundary."
"If there is a cause or condition that necessitates going out, one should not remain overnight.
At that time, in the village of the assembly, there was an elder named Udāyin; his family was very wealthy, possessing much property as well as clothing.
At that time, the elder prepared a great quantity of food and clothing within his home, setting them aside in a separate storehouse with the intention of making offerings to the community of bhikṣus.
He immediately dispatched a messenger to Śrāvastī to invite the community of bhikṣus, saying:
"In such-and-such a village, a certain elder has spoken as follows:"
"In my home, there is an abundance of clothing and food.
I now wish to make an offering to you, Venerable Sir!
I pray that you will deign to accept it out of compassion."
Then the bhikṣus asked the messenger,
"How far is that householder’s home from here? He replied:
"It is three *yojana*s from here.
The bhikṣus then thought to themselves:
"It is very far from here; if we wish to go, will we be able to return by evening?"
Each of them said, "Since it is so far from here, we will not be able to return by evening.
The World-Honored One has prescribed that we must observe the rains retreat and may not stay overnight outside the boundary; we do not know what to do."
He then did not go. At that time, there was another bhikṣu who was observing the rains retreat near that elephant village; he accepted the invitation.
Having accepted it, he obtained much clothing and food. When the three-month summer retreat was completed, he donned his robes, took up his bowl, and set out for Śrāvastī.
Traveling by degrees, he eventually reached that city and went to a monastery.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who came forward to welcome him, took his robes and bowl for him, and placed them inside the dwelling.
The host asked, "From where have you come?
Where do you reside?"
The guest replied, "We have recently been by the side of Hastigrāma; having completed the three-month rains retreat there, we have come from that place. The host asked:
“Was your rainy-season retreat harmonious, and did you not find it difficult to obtain almsfood?
They replied, “We spent the retreat there in great peace and happiness; our food and clothing were abundant, so we did not consider it a hardship.”
He then asked: "How is it that you were able to dwell there during the rainy season retreat with such abundance of food and clothing, without any lack?
They replied:

"In the vicinity of that place, there is a village named Hatthigāma. In that village there was an elder named Udena, whose family was immensely wealthy. With deep faith, he performed meritorious deeds, providing abundant food, drink, and clothing as gifts; it was because of this that [the community] was so well-provided for."
Then that bhikṣu spoke these words:
"Indeed, that householder also once came to invite me.
Furthermore, I asked him:"
"How far is it from here? He replied, "Three yojanas."
He thought to himself:
"If I go there, I fear I will not return before nightfall.
The World-Honored One does not permit one to stay overnight outside the boundaries of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) precinct."
"Thus, he did not go. At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:

"Although my śrāvaka disciples have no attachment to food or clothing, for the sake of enabling them to dwell in peace and happiness, and so that donors may obtain the merit of enjoyment, I should permit them to attend such invitations for a period of seven days."
Thereupon, he assembled the Saṃgha and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If, during the rainy season retreat, there is a matter that requires one to go outside the boundary, one should request a period of seven days down to a single day before departing."
When the Buddha ordered them to go, the bhikṣus did not know for what purpose they should go.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It refers to matters concerning upāsakas, upāsikās, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs."
Not knowing what constituted the duties of an upāsaka and so forth, the Buddha said:
"If there is business in the house of an upāsaka, he should take the robes he himself wears and prepare food and drink, then send a messenger to invite the bhikṣus: [text continues]"
“May the Venerable One please come to receive this offering.
This is called the duty of an upāsaka.
He should approach a single bhikṣu, squat down with palms joined, and undertake the seven-day rite before departing.
This is called the basis for a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
"If a lay follower wishes to give bedding and other requisites, as well as various kinds of food and clothing, to a bhikṣu, he addresses the bhikṣu, saying:
'I pray that the Noble Assembly will compassionately accept my gift of food and clothing.'"
The Buddha said: "A bhikṣu should observe the seven-day rule (saptāha-vidhi) when going outside the boundary.
This is called the occasion for an upāsaka."
"If there is an upāsaka who, because the bhikṣus lack food and drink, prepares many superior and delicious foods and drinks and comes to invite the bhikṣus."
The Buddha said:
"One should observe the seven-day rite (saptāha-vidhi) to go outside the boundary.
This is called the duty of an upāsaka."
"Furthermore, there is an upāsaka who has constructed a stūpa and wishes to install a relic (dhātu), having prepared various kinds of incense and flowers.
He comes to invite the bhikṣus, saying:
'I pray that the Venerable Ones will assist me in this meritorious deed.'"
The Buddha said: “A bhikṣu should accept and observe the seven-day rule before departing.
This is called the duty of an upāsaka as well as a service for the Buddha.”

"Furthermore, there are other upāsakas who construct stūpas and install their *cakra* wheels, or offer banners, flags, and parasols, or apply various fragrances such as sandalwood and saffron to the stūpas as offerings, as well as providing food, drink, and clothing."
"Come and invite the bhikṣus.
The Buddha said,
"You should go after having undertaken the seven-day rule."
This is called the duty of an upāsaka.
"If there is an upāsaka who either transcribes the sūtras and studies them, or transcribes the mātṛkās and studies them, as well as the words of all the Buddhas;..."
"Once it has been written, you wish to prepare an offering; come then and invite the bhikṣus.
The Buddha said, "You should go after having undertaken the seven-day rule."
This is called the duty of an upāsaka.

"If an upāsaka, regarding the concise exposition and all that remains doubtful, is unable to resolve them and wishes to ask a bhikṣu for the clarification of their meaning and phrasing, he may, for the purpose of removing those doubts, invite the bhikṣus by providing them with food and drink and receive permission to go outside the boundary for seven days."
This is called the lay follower (upāsaka) and his religious duties.
"If a lay follower should suddenly fall into wrong views and cease to believe in cause and effect, he may come to invite a bhikṣu to eliminate those wrong views."
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should accept and observe the seven-day rule to go beyond the boundary in order to eliminate wrong views.
This is called the matter concerning an upāsaka."

"If there is an upāsaka whose wife is pregnant and who, fearing the occurrence of calamity, desires to ensure the safety and well-being of both mother and child, he may come and request the Saṃgha to perform the 'bowl-covering' (pātrāvakṣepaṇa) offering."
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should accept and observe the seven-day rule before departing.
This is called the matter concerning an upāsaka."
"If a lay follower (upāsaka), on account of being ill, prepares various foods and drinks as well as garments, and comes to invite a bhikṣu, saying:
'I am afraid my life will end due to this illness; I wish to make an offering to the Saṃgha.'"
"Such a thing has occurred.
The Buddha said, "You may go,
having received the authorization for the seven-day rule."
This is called the matter of the upāsaka.
"What is the matter of the upāsikā?
It is as extensive as the matter of the upāsaka."
"What is the business of a bhikṣu?
It is when a bhikṣu constructs a dwelling and a grove and offers them to the Saṃgha of the four quarters;
for the sake of celebration, he provides various foods and drinks, as well as robes, to make offerings to the Saṃgha."

When messengers are sent to invite the bhikṣus at the appropriate time, the bhikṣus should accept the seven-day rule (*saptāha-vidhi*) and depart. This is called the "occasion for a bhikṣu. Furthermore, regarding the "occasion for a bhikṣu":

after having gifted a monastery (*ārāma*) to the bhikṣus, one further gifts bedding and furniture, and provides regular invitations for offerings; or constructs a stūpa for the *śarīra* (relics); or applies various fragrances such as sandalwood and saffron; or installs a *cakra* (wheel) on the spire, along with banners, flags, and parasols; and furthermore, makes offerings to the fourfold assembly and transcribes the sūtras.
When such circumstances as those mentioned above arise and invite [the presence of] bhikṣus, the bhikṣus should accept the seven-day rule (*saptāha-vidhi*) and depart.
This is called the "circumstance of the bhikṣu.

Furthermore, if there are bhikṣus who wish to discipline wicked persons by performing various formal acts (*karmavācanā*), and they invite the community of bhikṣus to provide assistance, the community of bhikṣus should accept the seven-day rule and depart.
This is called the "occasion for a bhikṣu.
If the community of bhikṣus wishes to discipline a wicked person by performing various formal acts (*karmas*), they come to invite a bhikṣu, saying:
"Come and assist us."
"A bhikṣu should accept and observe the seven-day rule before departing.
This is called the 'Bhikṣu-saṃgha-cause. If there is a bhikṣu..."
Afflicted by severe illness and suffering,
he sent a messenger to invite the bhikṣu,
saying: "Please preach the Dharma for me."
"And please come to see me.
The Buddha said,
"A bhikṣu should go by undertaking the seven-day rule (saptāha-vidhi)."
This is called the occasion for a bhikṣu.
What is the occasion for a bhikṣuṇī and others?

It is the same as that for a bhikṣu; however, the specific differences therein are: when making offerings to the saṃgha of bhikṣus, or making offerings to the Dharma, or giving material gifts at the proper time; and when those training in the Buddha’s Dharma, as well as śikṣamāṇā women who wish to receive full ordination (upasampadā), come to invite bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
"Please come and grant me full ordination.
At that time, the two assemblies should accept and observe the seven-day rule before departing.
This is known as the occasion concerning bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others.
"What is meant by 'the case of a śrāmaṇera'?
It is the same as the preceding rule.
What is meant by 'the case of a śrāmaṇerī'?"
The rest is as previously stated; the specific difference therein is that twelve young girls, having reached the age of eighteen, requested the community of bhikṣus:
"May you please confer upon us the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas."
"The bhikṣu should depart.
This is called the case concerning a śrāmaṇerī.
If a bhikṣu, having entered the rains retreat, should have this thought:
"I have entered this rainy-season retreat, yet no one provides me with food; I may well perish.
Or there may be those who have not yet studied the sūtras and ought to study them, or those who have previously practiced meditative concentration and ought to engage in reflection.
There may be those who have not yet realized what should be realized, who have not yet seen what they seek to see, or who have not yet attained what they seek to attain.
If such circumstances exist and one wishes to leave the dwelling place, the Buddha said:
"There is no offense."
"Nor does this constitute a breach of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat). If one has completed the *varṣā* and suddenly falls ill, and knows that there is no medicine or physician—
if he remains, his life may not be preserved— then departing due to such circumstances as the danger to life, the Buddha said:
"There is no offense, nor is the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) broken.
If a bhikṣu has completed his *varṣā* and falls ill, and although there is medicine available, there is no one to nurse him and he fears for his life, the Buddha said:
"I permit you to leave; the *varṣā* is not broken."
If a bhikṣu has completed his summer retreat (varṣā), and a woman comes to the bhikṣu’s dwelling and says:
“I have a daughter-in-law and a maidservant whom I wish to send to serve the Venerable One.”
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"If I do not go, I fear I shall lose my brahmacarya, and furthermore, life-threatening dangers and the like may arise.
This is what is meant by "conditions such as the loss of brahmacarya"; thus spoke the Buddha.
"One who departs incurs no offense and does not break the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat).
If there are circumstances involving men, eunuchs, or the like, one should depart accordingly as stated above.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has completed his *varṣā* and sees a woman and gives rise to lustful thoughts, and being unable to restrain his afflictions (*kleśa*), fears losing his pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), he should also depart."
If a bhikṣu has completed his rainy-season retreat and sees a hidden treasure, he should think:
"If I remain here, I fear I will be unable to restrain my mind and will take the object."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense in moving away.
If, during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), a relative or kinsman should suddenly come to advise a bhikṣu to remain in residence, [the bhikṣu may move].
If a bhikṣu, finding [the place] detestable or lowly, moves to another location, he is without fault, as previously stated.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu is invited by women, men, or paṇḍakas to observe the *varṣā* retreat;

Having accepted that invitation, it may be that this donor has incurred debts to others, or has killed another person, or has plundered the property of others; or perhaps at the dwelling place there are tigers, wolves, lions, or other such fierce beasts and calamities that come to terrify the donor, causing him to flee or even to die.
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:

"This donor has invited me to observe the rains retreat; yet, as before, various difficulties have arisen. If I remain here now, there may come conditions through which I might lose my brahmacarya or even my life."
Regarding those who move to another location for the rains retreat (*varṣā*), there is no offense, as previously stated.
If, however, at the place where one is staying, many causes of illness and suffering arise such that the bhikṣu finds it unpleasant to remain there, the Buddha said:
"Move to another location for the rains retreat; there is no offense, as previously stated."

Furthermore, if a woman, man, or *paṇḍaka* should come and invite a bhikṣu to enter the rains retreat with them, and a king should then seize that donor, or kill him, or plunder his wealth, at which time the donor flees to another place.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This donor has encountered such terror that he has already fled.
If I remain here, I may lose my brahmacarya or face other perils such as threats to my life."
If he moves to another location,
as before, there is no offense.
If a donor comes and invites a bhikṣu to enter the rains retreat, [he may go].
However, this donor’s house suddenly caught fire, and he either died or fled.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This donor has now suddenly encountered fire; he is either dead or has run away."
"I am dwelling here alone; I fear there may be danger to my life as well as to my holy life (brahmacarya).
If he moves to another location, as before, there is no offense.
If a donor comes to invite a bhikṣu to perform the practice of the rainy-season retreat (varṣā), [he may accept].
If the dwelling place is low-lying and damp with much water, one should fear that illness may arise later;
moving to another location is, as before, without offense.
If a donor comes to invite a bhikṣu to perform the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), [the same applies].
However, while at his dwelling place, he spoke disparagingly:
"What is the use of staying here with a shaven head, undergoing the suffering of hunger, and living beneath forest trees?
You should return home, perform many meritorious deeds, and there is no need to leave the household life."
The bhikṣu reflects:
"If I remain for long, I may lose my brahmacarya.
If such a condition exists, he is permitted to depart without fault.
If, during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), a king should arrive with his fourfold army and come to the bhikṣu’s dwelling place, dispatching men to seize the bhikṣu and speak thus:

"You shall be conscripted for labor according to secular law, or compelled to return to lay life, or forced to marry a wife, or deprived of your robes and bowl, or subjected to various forms of harassment."
If such an obstacle arises, one may depart immediately without fault, and it does not constitute a violation of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat).
If, at the residence of a bhikṣu, there are men, women, or *paṇḍakas* who come to invite the bhikṣu to observe the *varṣā* and provide him with clothing and food;
Later, when difficulties arose from kings and others, they all fled on their own, and no one provided them with support.
For this reason, it is not an offense for a bhikṣu to go elsewhere.
If, during the rainy season retreat (varṣā), bandits arrive and commit various illegal acts, such as stealing oxen, sheep, and other livestock, or slaughtering them; [This concludes the section.]
If such an evil thief comes to where the bhikṣus are and says, "You all get out;
I wish to stay here," and if there is such a wicked robber who comes into the monastery to disturb the bhikṣus, one should simply leave immediately; there is no offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu enters the rains retreat depending upon a male, a female, or a eunuch as his patron.
At that time, that patron is seized by others, bound by enemies, or terrified by non-human beings, and flees to another region, whereupon he passes away.
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"In this present retreat, there are many afflictions and obstacles, and we have no further donors.
Due to these circumstances, our holy life will be impaired."
If, due to difficult circumstances involving śramaṇas, one moves to another location, there is no offense of breaking the summer retreat (varṣā-bheda).
Wherever one arrives, one may enter the formal retreat (anujñāta-varṣā).
Having entered the retreat at that very place, one must not cross the boundary (sīmā).

Furthermore, there were previously dwelling places of non-humans where bhikṣus entered the rains retreat; ignorant people, such as the elderly and children, entered these temples and discharged impurities, making them unfit for proximity.
Furthermore, near a river, the waters swelled and overflowed, causing the loss of the donor’s household goods and clothing; some died and others fled.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This donor has encountered this calamity of the waters."
"If I remain here, there will certainly arise obstacles to my life or to the holy life.
Moving to another location is likewise without offense, as previously stated.

If, during the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), a monk sees another monk instructing yet another monk to perform acts that cause a schism in the Saṃgha, or to exhort others toward such ends, or to employ the means for causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
Then that bhikṣu thought to himself:

"At this very place, there is currently a matter of schism within the Saṃgha. If I were to observe the rains retreat here, those bhikṣus would seek to cause a schism, or they would instruct others to do so, or incite them to it, and employ various expedient means."
Again, he thought: "I have now offered this well-spoken exhortation, yet he will certainly not accept it and will treat me with hostility.
If I remain here for long, such a situation will arise."
"One who has already studied will surely forget it, and one who has not yet studied cannot be made to progress; therefore, it is not appropriate to remain here.
If one moves elsewhere to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) there, as before, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, during the rainy season retreat, hears that another bhikṣu intends to perform an act that would cause a schism in the Saṃgha,
and that bhikṣu is his close friend or spiritual mentor, he should think: "If I follow his words,
I fear there will be an act of schism in the Saṃgha and I shall incur an offense."
If one does not accept the invitation, yet it is from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*),
one should observe the seven-day limit and go outside the boundary.
If the matter is not resolved within those seven days, there is no offense in exceeding them.
If one does not leave, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

If there is a bhikṣu who hears another bhikṣu say that by observing the three-month rains retreat in another location, one gains much material benefit, and this bhikṣu then desires to observe the rains retreat there; [he must inform his preceptor or teacher.]
Furthermore, another bhikṣu said:
"There is gain and support here, and there is also gain and support there.
Since it is the same in both places, it would not be worth going there."
"A bhikṣu who observes the rains retreat here will consequently fail to obtain gains.
Yet that person previously stated that such a bhikṣu would incur an offense against the Dharma.
If a bhikṣu hears another bhikṣu say:
"There is a place where one may observe the rains retreat.

The bhikṣu then went there, and after participating in the counting of voting sticks (*śalākā*), he was unable to obtain any of the items he was entitled to receive; that bhikṣu who had made the initial statement incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*)."
If there is a bhikṣu who hears other bhikṣus say,
"In such-and-such a residence, there was a place for the three-month summer retreat," and having heard this,
he goes there, participates in the counting of voting-sticks (śalākā), but fails to obtain bedding and is unable to remain, that bhikṣu is said to have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu hears another bhikṣu say, "In such-and-such a place,
there will be a place for the three-month rains retreat," he immediately goes there;
having participated in the counting of ballots and received his share of bedding and furniture, he then departs elsewhere.
If one does not remain in residence at another location, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense and the rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*) is not validly established.
If a bhikṣu hears another bhikṣu say:
"In such-and-such a dwelling place, there is a site for the three-month rainy-season retreat."

At that time, he departed and participated in the distribution of bedding by receiving a tally. Having completed the *varṣā* retreat, he had personal business and left the boundary without taking up the seven-day permission; thus, his prior *varṣā* was not valid, and he incurred an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
If a bhikṣu hears another bhikṣu say, "In such-and-such a residence, there will be a place for the three-month rains retreat," he immediately goes there.

Having arrived, he enters the rains retreat, receives his tally, and the bedding and furniture have been distributed. Then, having a reason, he takes up the seven-day leave and goes outside the boundary, and does not observe the three-month rains retreat in that residence.
By speaking as previously mentioned, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu who has undertaken the seven-day observance does not return after the seven days have passed, his *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is broken.
However, these six types of *pūrvavārṣika* (early rains) procedures do not differ from the *paścimavārṣika* (later rains) procedures; they are all performed according to the *pūrvavārṣika* model.
The only difference is that the term "the latter three months" is used; the rest is as explained in detail in the *Ekottarakarma*.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda: Matters Concerning the Vassa Retreat, One Scroll.
